content: Cauliflower ear, also known as hematoma auris or perichondrial hematoma, is a condition frequently observed in individuals who participate in contact sports such as wrestling, rugby, and mixed martial arts, as well as in boxers from the 1920s. When the external portion of the ear sustains trauma, blood or other fluids can accumulate beneath the perichondrium, the connective tissue layer that supplies nutrients to the cartilage. This separation of the cartilage from its nutrient source can lead to cartilage necrosis. As a result, the outer ear becomes permanently swollen and deformed, taking on an appearance reminiscent of a cauliflower. To prevent this condition, protective headgear designed to shield the ears is commonly used in wrestling, martial arts, and other contact sports. When fluid accumulation occurs in the outer ear, it is critical to seek immediate medical attention. A physician will drain the fluid and apply a compressive dressing to the outer ear to reattach the perichondrium to the cartilage. This compressive dressing must remain in place for approximately 10 days to prevent recurrent fluid buildup. Due to the susceptibility of the outer ear to infections, antibiotics are typically prescribed as a precautionary measure. If the condition is left untreated, significant damage to the ear can occur. Persistent pressure may lead to the rupture of the eardrum, which can exacerbate the deformity of the ear, causing further wrinkling and a pale appearance, hence the term cauliflower ear. In cases where the eardrum ruptures, the only available treatment involves suturing the wound to facilitate healing. However, even with appropriate medical intervention, substantial hearing loss may still occur. Modern cosmetic procedures are available to enhance the external appearance of the ear, although internal damage caused by the condition remains irreversible.
